⁉️ Charles Schwab has expanded its cryptocurrency trading service to include Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink, allowing eligible US retail investors to buy and sell five digital assets directly through Schwab Crypto. Schwab said its selection of cryptocurrencies is based on customer demand and its preference for established digital assets. The company intends to introduce more tokens and other digital asset products over time, although it has not identified the next cryptocurrencies it plans to support.

The eighth survival rule.

Bolting the door and stockpiling food in the living room does not make your home a safe fortress. Most people who lost their lives inside their homes during the Bosnian War and hurricane disasters did so because they did not know 'how to fortify a home.'

Five ironclad rules of home defense for avoiding becoming a target for looters and protecting your family and shelter to the very end.

1. Blind faith in door locks and front doors: Doors are breached through the 'door frame.'

Even the latest digital door locks or auxiliary locks can be ripped off in 15 seconds with a single steel pry bar (crowbar). Looters do not pick the lock; they use a pry bar to break the door hinges and door frame (strike plate) and force their way in.
The key to protecting your door is not an expensive lock, but long steel screws at least 7.5 cm long that anchor the door frame deep into the wall, and a steel security bar placed under the door.

2. Lights at night are 'lighthouses' that attract snipers and looters.

A city without power is pitch-black at night. In those conditions, a single candle or the glow of a smartphone screen in the living room can cast your silhouette through the curtains for up to 1 km.
It is effectively advertising to the entire neighborhood: "This house still has batteries, candles, and supplies."
At night, cover windows completely with aluminum foil emergency blankets or blackout tape to achieve 100% blackout, and use only red light or a tiny lantern pointed at the floor.

3. Cooking smells are 'pheromones' that turn hungry neighbors into looters.

After 4–5 days without electricity and with grocery stores stripped bare, people become extremely sensitive to hunger.
At that point, the smell of meat cooking or warm instant noodles boiling in the kitchen spreads throughout the building through vents and hallways.
The moment they catch the scent, even a neighbor who was normally kind becomes an intruder knocking on your door to survive. For the first 1–2 weeks of a crisis, you must get by without cooking or making any smells, using non-heated food (peanut butter, energy bars, canned food eaten cold).

4. The trap of standing watch by the window: Do not stand guard; become a 'shadow.'

Standing by a window with a gun or blunt weapon, looking outside, is not vigilance—it is suicide.
From outside, your head and shoulder silhouette against the window frame is clearly visible in the darkness. You become a perfect target for rocks or gunfire.
Do not observe the outside from right beside the window. Instead, stay behind a dark corner farther inside the room and look out at an angle, or use a small mirror to keep your body hidden while maintaining a view.

5. No protection against arson: A fortress without a fire extinguisher is a 'wood-burning stove.'

If an intruder cannot break through the door, what is the easiest tactic they can use? Setting fire to the ground floor, beneath the front door, or on the balcony.
No matter how impenetrable a fortress you build, once it fills with smoke and toxic gases, you will have to crawl out within 10 minutes.
Fortifying a home without a dry chemical fire extinguisher in every room, a gas mask with a filter cartridge, wet towels, and an escape rope is like trapping yourself in a mousetrap. You must secure an escape route at the back (a rear window or the roof).

Conclusion:
The safest home against looters is not an 'impenetrable steel fortress.'
It is one disguised as an 'empty house whose door has already been broken down and looted, making it look like there is nothing left worth taking.'
The greatest defense is not winning a fight, but never catching their eye in the first place.

SoftBank is probably best known for its stories involving WeWork and some of the world's biggest companies. And it looks like the holding company has now reached a point where AI is no longer just a story about rising asset valuations, but a story about real debt.

The company has made a massive bet on AI. It has invested or committed to invest around $65 billion in OpenAI alone, while OpenAI and Arm now account for roughly three-quarters of the value of its key assets.

The problem is that a significant portion of this bet is being financed with debt. In September, SoftBank issued $11.1 billion in bonds, the largest high-yield corporate bond offering in history. Some of those bonds carried yields of nearly 10% annually.

And the market is already getting nervous. SoftBank shares have lost nearly half their value since the beginning of September, while the cost of insuring against a potential debt default has reached its highest level in four years.

The really uncomfortable part begins if AI asset valuations continue to fall. That would mean collateral loses value, borrowing becomes more expensive, and the company may have to sell assets to reduce its debt. And SoftBank owns a significant stake in Arm, is one of OpenAI's largest investors, and is financing massive AI infrastructure projects.

That's why SoftBank's problems could quickly stop being the problems of just one company. 
The pressure could spread to Arm, private AI company valuations, data centers, and eventually the entire tech market.

On Tuesday, November 10, SoftBank will release its latest quarterly earnings report. The main things to watch are its debt, cash position, and how the company plans to keep financing its AI bet.

Because if the next major AI crisis starts not with a stock market sell-off, but with debt problems at the biggest borrowers, SoftBank is one of the first places to look for signs of trouble.
